extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants, prosecuting attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on evaluating and presenting secondary considerations (objective indicia) of nonobviousness during patent prosecution, including commercial success, long‑felt need, copying, skepticism of experts, enablement/utility affidavits, and procedures to disqualify prior art. Focused on what evidence is probative and how to assess nexus, scope, and provenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison for unexpected results must be against the closest prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of unexpected results must compare the claimed invention with the closest prior art; applicant is not required to compare with subject matter that does not exist in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An applicant need not test all compounds taught by each reference, but tests of less than all must be sufficient to permit a conclusion respecting the relative effectiveness of applicant’s claimed compounds and the compounds of the closest prior art (citing In re Johnson; In re Payne). Cases cited: In re Geiger; In re Chapman. The record must show comparison to the most relevant prior art rather than hypothetical combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration or affidavit form requirement for evidentiary assurances
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence offered to prove factual assertions should be presented in declaration or affidavit form to obtain statutory assurances of correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring declaration/affidavit form ensures statements are correct under 35 U.S.C. 25 and 18 U.S.C. 1001; publications may be considered to the extent probative but may not substitute for required affidavits where the statute demands them (Ex parte Gray).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages disclosed or inherent may be considered even if not in specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence and arguments directed to advantages not disclosed in the specification cannot be disregarded; such advantages may rebut a prima facie case of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Totality of the record is relevant (In re Chu). Undisclosed properties that flow from disclosed use (e.g., minimized side effects) must be considered (In re Zenitz; Ex parte Sasajima).

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the record governs obviousness; consider prosecution give-and-take
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness is determined by the totality of the record including evidence and arguments developed during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no rule that evidence traversing a §103 rejection must be contained in the specification; prosecution history, affidavits, and other evidence may be probative (In re Chu).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus requirement between claimed invention and commercial success
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant asserting commercial success must establish a factually and legally sufficient connection (nexus) between the evidence of commercial success and the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burden of proof rests on applicant to provide 'hard evidence' of commercial success and nexus in ex parte prosecution (In re Huang; In re GPAC; In re Paulsen). The term 'nexus' designates a connection so the evidence is probative (Demaco Corp.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success abroad is relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success in foreign markets is relevant to the issue of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of commercial success abroad may be considered along with U.S. success (Lindemann Maschinenfabrik v. American Hoist & Derrick Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success must be commensurate in scope with the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence of commercial success must be commensurate in scope with the claims; success attributable to unclaimed features is not probative of nonobviousness of the claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence showing success of narrower or different products/processes is not necessarily commensurate with broader claims (In re Tiffin; Joy Technologies v. Manbeck). An affidavit merely stating a product is 'constructed according to the disclosure and claims' does not establish nexus because it does not show the sold product corresponds to the claimed invention (Ex parte Standish).

rubrics_metrics.name: When claimed invention not coextensive with commercial product, show legal relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: If the commercial product/process is not coextensive with the claims, applicant must show a legally sufficient relationship between the claimed feature and the commercial product or process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant need not show commercial success at every point in a claimed range if substantial success at a typical point is shown and affidavits indicate operation throughout approximates that point (In re Hollingsworth; Demaco Corp.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success must be derived from the claimed invention (not advertising/business factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success must be shown to be directly derived from the claimed features, not from heavy promotion, advertising, brand loyalty, pricing, or other extraneous business factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusive assertions by inventor as to purchaser motives are insufficient; licensing and advertising must be carefully appraised because these may account for success (In re Mageli; In re Noznick; Pentec v. Graphic Controls; Hybritech v. Monoclonal Antibodies). In ex parte proceedings applicant must show claimed features were responsible if the evidence is to be accorded substantial weight (In re Huang).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success must flow from functions/advantages disclosed or inherent in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The commercial success of devices within the claims must flow from functions and advantages disclosed or inherent in the specification, not from modifications by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success attributable to improvements or modifications made by others is not probative (In re Vamco Machine & Tool, Inc.). Ensure the linkage to disclosed/inherent properties is demonstrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus is especially difficult to establish in design cases
rubrics_metrics.description: In design patent or design-related claim contexts, evidence of commercial success must be clearly attributable to the design itself rather than brand recognition, improved performance, or other factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate that consumers purchased for the design; mere market leadership or brand strength may undermine a nexus finding (Litton Systems v. Whirlpool).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sales figures must be adequately defined and contextualized
rubrics_metrics.description: Gross sales figures alone do not show commercial success unless accompanied by evidence of market share, time period, or expected sales in the market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide market share data, relevant timeframes, and comparators; unsupported gross sales are insufficient (Cable Electric Products v. Genmark; Ex parte Standish).

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-felt need and failure of others: existence and persistence required
rubrics_metrics.description: To support nonobviousness, the claimed invention must satisfy a long‑felt need that was recognized, persistent, and not previously solved by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Need must be objective and recognized by those of ordinary skill; if a prior art product satisfied the need before applicant's invention, long-felt need is negated (In re Gershon; Newell Companies v. Kenney Mfg.). Evidence of prior unsuccessful attempts by others strengthens the factor (Orthopedic Equipment Co. v. All Orthopedic Appliances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-felt need is measured from the date the problem was identified and efforts made
rubrics_metrics.description: The analysis of long-felt need is as of the date the problem was identified and efforts were made to solve it, not the date of the most pertinent prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish when the problem was recognized and contemporaneous attempts to solve it (Texas Instruments v. ITC).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider other contributing factors to apparent failure of others
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent failure of others to solve a problem may be due to lack of interest or appreciation rather than lack of technical know‑how; such context must be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits by licensees and evidence of bona fide market interest can add weight (In re Tiffin; Scully Signal Co.; Environmental Designs v. Union Oil).

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism of experts is strong evidence of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions of disbelief or skepticism by experts, especially when contemporaneous and prior to the invention, constitute strong evidence supporting nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemporaneous expert skepticism and prolonged research efforts preceding the invention are entitled to evidentiary weight (Environmental Designs; In re Dow Chemical Co.; Burlington Industries v. Quigg).

rubrics_metrics.name: Copying is a secondary consideration but requires more than mere imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that competitors copied the invention may support nonobviousness, but more than mere copying is necessary; copying may be due to other motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copying persuasive when an alleged infringer expended substantial effort over time and, after failing, copied the claimed invention (Dow Chem. Co. v. American Cyanamid). Not persuasive where copies are non‑identical or the competitor had not tried to develop its own solution (Pentec; Vandenberg; Panduit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inoperability of references: presumption of operability and burden to rebut
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are presumed valid and operable; affidavits attacking operability of a cited patent/reference must rebut the presumption of operability by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should not opine on operability; mere demonstration that one can practice within a disclosure without obtaining the alleged product does not overcome the presumption (Metropolitan Eng. Co. v. Coe; In re Weber). Failures by uninterested experimenters carry little weight. If inoperability is asserted for features not relied upon, the reference remains effective for operative features (In re Shepherd).

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility and operability of applicant’s disclosure: when to require and evaluate evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on when it is proper to require evidence of utility or operability and how to evaluate submitted evidence to overcome lack of utility under 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to MPEP § 2107.02 and related sections for criteria and precedents. Examiners may require evidence when appropriate and should evaluate the sufficiency of affidavits or proofs presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of disclosure (enablement) and burden after prima facie rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Once examiner establishes a prima facie case of lack of enablement, the burden falls on applicant to present persuasive arguments and suitable proofs that one skilled in the art could make and use the invention from the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits or declarations cannot establish facts that the specification itself should recite (In re Buchner; In re Smyth). Evidence supplementing a deficient specification must show that missing information was known to those of skill in the art (In re Howarth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavits/declarations explaining or interpreting disclosure are usually not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits or declarations that merely state a claim is 'disclosed' are generally not given weight; testimony that explains underlying factual basis for an opinion about disclosure may be admissible and weighed case‑by‑case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opinion testimony asserting disclosure should be evaluated cautiously; the Board has admitted explanatory expert testimony that sets out factual bases (In re Oppenauer; Glaser v. Strickland). Weight is evaluated strictly on a case‑by‑case basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution affidavits/declarations may disqualify a reference when successful
rubrics_metrics.description: Under certain circumstances an affidavit/declaration may attribute a reference (article, patent, published application) to the applicant, thereby preventing the reference from being used as prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If successful, the subject matter is no longer applicable as prior art. Applicants may submit evidence under 37 CFR 1.131 or 1.132 to show prior invention or derivation (see MPEP § 715). An unequivocal statement by the applicant about inventorship may be accepted, but may not suffice where contrary evidence exists (In re Katz; In re DeBaun; Ex parte Kroger; In re Carreira).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.130(a) requirements to disqualify commonly owned patent/publication as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: When a §103 rejection relies on a U.S. patent or patent application publication that is not prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(b) and the inventions are commonly owned and not patentably distinct, the applicant/owner may disqualify that reference by submitting a terminal disclaimer and an oath/declaration stating common ownership and that the inventor named is the prior inventor under 35 U.S.C. 104.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 CFR 1.130(a)(1) requires a terminal disclaimer (37 CFR 1.321(c)); 1.130(a)(2) requires an oath/declaration including that the inventor of the application under examination is the prior inventor. The affidavit/declaration may be signed by inventor(s), attorney/agent of record, or assignee(s). See also limits on establishing dates of invention in foreign countries (NAFTA/WTO date limitations). Successful 1.132 affidavits do not allow stepping into the prior author's publication date to defeat another reference (In re Costello).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on establishing prior invention dates in foreign countries
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may not establish a date of invention in certain foreign countries for purposes of prior inventor claims earlier than specified treaty dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The phrase 'prior inventor under 35 U.S.C. 104' disallows establishing a date of invention in a foreign country other than a NAFTA or WTO member; and contains specific earliest dates for WTO/NAFTA countries (e.g., no earlier than Jan 1, 1996 for WTO country other than NAFTA; no earlier than Dec 8, 1993 for NAFTA country other than the U.S.).

rubrics_metrics.name: File wrapper contents and handling rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers that do not become a permanent part of the record should not be entered onto the 'Contents' of the file wrapper; papers legally entered are numbered and should not be expunged except with special authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 CFR 1.59 permits expungement in limited circumstances (unintentional submissions or proprietary info not important to patentability). Copies/duplicates handling rules: duplicates are usually destroyed unless timing requires retention. At allowance, only papers required by the printer are placed in the left/center section. Prints of drawings are fastened by the Office of Initial Patent Examination; white paper prints kept on top. See IFW manual cross‑references.
